extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, literary critics, dramatic poets and playwrights
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical-aesthetic guidance on composing and judging tragedy and comedy, and on the epistemic status and value of history versus poetry/science. Covers criteria for characterisation, unity, motive-structure, the spectator's effect, and the proper aims of historical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character embodiment (ventriloquism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poets 'transform themselves into each of the persons to be represented, and speak out of each of them like ventriloquists;' second‑rank poets 'transform the principal person to be represented into themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: Shakespeare and Goethe (inhabit each role with equal truth and naturalness). Anti‑pattern: poets who project their own personality onto the principal character (example given: Byron), producing lifeless secondary characters and an unconvincing dramatis personae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect is the sublime, not the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in tragedy belongs to the sense of the sublime: tragedy presents the terrible side of life and lifts us 'above the will and its interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: like the dynamical sublime, tragedy causes a turning away from the will. The tragic catastrophe should produce a feeling comparable to aesthetic sublimity (references: chord of the seventh, colour analogies) rather than mere beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy ought to awaken resignation (turning away from the will)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate tendency and end of tragedy is 'the awakening of the knowledge that the world, life, can afford us no true pleasure' and thereby a turning away of the will from life (resignation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effect may appear in the hero's mind (hero becomes resigned) or only in the spectator (spectator is led to resignation). Tragedy that fails to evoke this elevated resignation misses its true end; examples discuss ancient vs Christian/modern expressions of resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action is paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: The neglect of unity of time and place is only a fault if it destroys the unity of the action; unity of action is the essential unity demanded of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted: deviation in time/place so long as the action's unity remains intact. Anti‑pattern: violations of unity that leave only the unity of a principal character (example: instances where unity of action is lost). French classical strictness (single thing spoken of throughout) is contrasted with broader approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth allowed to reveal character (Shakespearean model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic work may include speeches or whole scenes that do not strictly advance the plot but give breadth and reveal characters or circumstances, enriching understanding of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespearean 'line with breadth' (exspatiatur) is defended against geometrical, narrowly focused dramas. Use such breadth deliberately to deepen representation of human nature; avoid gratuitous digressions that undermine the action's unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner economy of motives and tragic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: A highly perfect tragedy displays 'tragic disposition of the motives, tragic progress of the action, and tragic development' that culminates in the proper effect on the hero and spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example praised: the opera 'Norma' for its clear motivation and the musical indication of the hero's change of will. Scoring note: judge works by how coherently motives are arranged and how naturally the action progresses to the catastrophic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic poet should mirror the human race (varied characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic/epic poet is 'the mirror of the human race' and should represent many bad, profligate, foolish, buffoonish, and eccentric persons, with magnanimous characters being the rare exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: populate dramas with a realistic distribution of character types rather than an excess of heroic magnanimity (criticises works with 'too much and too universal magnanimity'). Examples: Homer and Shakespeare typically lack transcendent magnanimity; Goldoni is praised for balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose characters of sufficient social/political magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of great power and consideration are best adapted for tragedy because 'the fall is greatest from a height' and misfortune on that scale appears unconditionally terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: civic/low‑status tragedy is not to be unconditionally rejected but risks lacking the 'height to fall from' that produces terror in a broad audience; choose rank to match intended tragic magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's aesthetic aim: affirmation and amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy, as the opposite of tragedy, incites the continued assertion of the will: it presents suffering as passing and resolves into joy, asserting that life is 'thoroughly good' and 'always amusing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form: comedy should display the burlesque and laughable aspects of life, keep the spectator in good humour, and typically 'drop the curtain at the moment of joy' so subsequent reality does not complicate the affirmation. Anti‑pattern: treating comic adversity as permanent or concluding on an ambiguous downbeat undermines comedic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical method: history is not a science but deals with particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: History lacks the 'fundamental characteristic of science'—subordination of particulars under objective general conceptions—and so it is not a science but a co‑ordination of innumerable individuals and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: historians must accept that their object is the particular and contingent (the once‑only); historical knowledge is often imperfect and fragmentary, and general summaries in history are 'subjective generalities' not true objective conceptions. Scoring note: evaluate historical claims with awareness of limited predictive/explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of history: rational, collective self‑consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: History's special and proper province is to serve as 'the rational consciousness of the human race'—it gives a nation self‑knowledge by connecting present with past and thereby completes collective reason via writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing and preserving history restores unity to the race's consciousness and helps nations understand themselves; assess histories by how well they fulfill this function (clarity of connection between past and present, preservation of collective memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleological/constructive (Hegelian) histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive histories that 'comprehend the history of the world as a planned whole' or 'construe it organically' are criticised as based on crude realism and optimism which improperly take phenomena as inner being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: imposing a preconceived plan or teleology (ending in a 'rich, fat State' or inevitable moral progress). Guidance: historians should resist elevating temporal, contingent ends into eternal absolutes; avoid fashionable 'system‑building' that masks contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of history should seek the unchanging (the Ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosophy of history 'ought to fix its attention upon that which always is and never becomes nor passes away'—to recognise the identical element across all events (the permanent human qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological implication: interpret historical multiplicity as 'Eadem, sed aliter' (the same but different). Focus on identifying recurring human motives and qualities rather than narrating an overarching teleological development.
